findings.title: JWT 'none' Algorithm Allowed — Authentication Bypass
findings.description: The refactored jwt.decode() call passes algorithms=['RS256','none']. The 'none' algorithm tells PyJWT to accept tokens with no signature, allowing an attacker to forge arbitrary tokens (e.g., with any user ID or elevated role) and bypass authentication entirely. This is a well-known JWT vulnerability (CVE-2015-9235 class). The PR description claims 'functionally equivalent' — it is not; this is a severe security regression.
findings.remediation: Remove 'none' from the algorithms list. Use algorithms=['RS256'] exclusively. Consider also pinning with options={'require': ['exp', 'iat']} to enforce claim presence.
findings.cwe: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

findings.title: Expiry Check Removed — Replay Attack Window Opened
findings.description: The original code explicitly checked payload.get('exp', 0) < time.time() and rejected expired tokens. The new code relies solely on PyJWT's built-in exp verification inside the try/except block. If PyJWT is misconfigured (e.g., options={'verify_exp': False}) or a future caller overrides decode options, expired tokens will silently be accepted. The removal of the explicit guard also makes the intent less auditable.
findings.remediation: Restore the explicit expiry check after jwt.decode(), or at minimum add options={'require': ['exp']} to the decode call to force PyJWT to always validate expiry.

findings.title: Broad Exception Catch May Mask Unexpected Failures
findings.description: Catching jwt.InvalidTokenError and returning False silently swallows all JWT errors (malformed, wrong key, expired, etc.) as a simple auth failure with no logging. This makes security incidents and misconfiguration harder to detect or alert on.
findings.remediation: Log the exception (at WARN or ERROR level, without leaking the raw token) before returning False so that anomalous patterns can be observed in audit logs.
findings.cwe: CWE-390: Detection of Error Condition Without Action

output.summary: PR #215 claims to be a functionally equivalent refactor but introduces two critical security regressions: (1) 'none' is added to jwt.decode's allowed algorithms, enabling unsigned token forgery, and (2) the explicit expiry check is silently dropped. The author's description ('functionally equivalent') is factually wrong. Policy already flagged critical (auth_payment_critical). This must be blocked.

issues.comment: 'none' added to jwt.decode algorithms list. The JWT 'none' algorithm means no signature is required; any attacker can craft an arbitrary payload, base64-encode it, and submit it without a signature. Libraries that respect 'none' will accept it as valid. This is the canonical JWT algorithm-confusion attack (CVE-2015-9235). Must be reverted to algorithms=['RS256'] only.

The expiry check (`if payload.get('exp', 0) < time.time(): return False`) is removed with no explanation. jwt.decode does not enforce 'exp' by default in all library versions; explicitly checking it was a defence-in-depth measure. Its removal means expired tokens are now accepted indefinitely, breaking session revocation and any logout mechanism that relies on token expiry.

tests/auth/test_session.py is listed as changed but no diff is visible. Cannot verify whether tests cover the two regressions. Given the nature of the changes, tests for (a) 'none'-algorithm tokens being rejected and (b) expired tokens being rejected are mandatory before any approval.

Adding a try/except around jwt.decode to catch InvalidTokenError is the only defensible change in this diff and should be preserved in a corrected version. However, it does not offset the blockers above.
